blocks.text: The lament over Babylon is voiced by kings, merchants, and those who profit from sea trade, but their grief centers on the loss of wealth and customers. The cargo list moves from costly luxury goods to enslaved people and “souls of men,” exposing an economy in which even human lives are treated as merchandise. This reading sees the chapter’s judgment as directed not simply at a city’s splendor, but at the destructive system of wealth and trade associated with it.

A common but disputed reading understands “Babylon” in Revelation’s first-century setting as referring to Rome, while also drawing on biblical Babylon imagery to criticize imperial city-power. On this view, the chapter is not limited to one named ruler: it portrays the interwoven force of imperial power, civic religion, and economy. Revelation’s repeated reworking of Israel’s Scriptures helps explain why its images can speak through the name “Babylon” rather than by naming its target directly.
